newsitem.title: USA: Trial results may broaden Taxol availability.
newsitem.headline: Trial results may broaden Taxol availability.

text.p: The latest trial results of a therapy involving Taxol, considered a potential breakthrough in treating cancer, could mean broader availability of the product in Europe, a Bristol-Myers Squibb Inc official based in Paris said Tuesday.

Michel Pettigrew, vice president and general manager of the U.S. drug company's oncology division in Europe, said in a telephone interview that many healthcare systems in the continent were waiting for those results.

He confirmed that the trial results from a study conducted in Europe and Canada which involved patients with advanced ovarian cancer reaffirmed some of the benefits shown in an earlier study last year called GOG-111.
In the most recent tests, Taxol, a yew-tree extract whose synthetic version is registered to Bristol-Myers, was combined with cisplatin, which is also used in ovarian therapy.
Taxol has been available in Europe for three and a half years, he said, but is not yet available in the U.S.

In the 16-month trial involving 680 patients, results showed that ovarian cancer in patients who were given Taxol and cisplatin did not progress for 16.6 months compared with 12 months for those receiving cisplatin plus cyclophosphamide, according to a report released at a meeting of the American Society of Clinical Oncology in Denver on Tuesday.

Pettigrew noted that the three-hour dosing schedule in the latest tests as against 24 hours in GOG-111 opens the possibility that the therapy could be used for outpatient purposes, which could produce savings for healthcares systems.
Pettigrew cautioned that the study is not yet complete, confirming a statement by Martine Piccart, who released the results, that survival data still needs to be completed and analyzed.

Pettigrew noted that in Europe, it would be up to regulatory agencies to determine later on whether, as a first line drug, a further change of labeling may be introduced. Such change may result in shorter-time of infusion and slightly higher dosing, he noted.
Commenting on the cancer-fighting potentials of Taxol, he noted that, "we've barely scratched the surface."
